title: Regression: Predicting Numbers
subtitle: What is a house worth? Linear regression as the interpretable baseline, coefficients in dollars, log targets, ridge and lasso, and the residual plot that tells you what the model is missing

objectives.title: Fit and Read a Linear Regression
objectives.description: Coefficients are slopes in business units: $112 per square foot, $9,800 per garage bay. You'll learn to state them, to standardize them before comparing them, and to stop reading them as causes.

objectives.title: Pick the Right Error Metric
objectives.description: RMSE punishes big misses, MAE reports the typical miss, MAPE explodes near zero, R² tells you how much of the variance you explained. Which one you report depends on who is asking.

objectives.title: Regularize With Ridge, Lasso & Elastic Net
objectives.description: Eighty features, one thousand houses: the recipe for overfitting. Penalized regression shrinks coefficients — and lasso sets most of them to exactly zero, which is feature selection for free.

objectives.title: Diagnose With Residuals
objectives.description: Predicted vs. actual, residuals vs. fitted, and the fan shape that says 'take the log of the target.' The plots that separate a model that works from one that merely runs.

agenda.title: From Yes/No to How Much
agenda.description: Classification predicts a label; regression predicts a number — a price, a demand, a delivery time, a lifetime value. Same lifecycle, different target, different metrics. The Ames housing data: 1,460 sales, 79 features, a median price of $163,000.
bulletPoints: The baseline is the mean: predict $181K for every house, RMSE ≈ $74K. Every model must beat that
Sale price is right-skewed: a few $500K+ homes will dominate squared error unless we take the log

agenda.title: One Feature, One Line
agenda.description: Price against living area. The least-squares line, the intercept, the slope, and what 'holding everything else fixed' means once we add a second feature. The whole of linear regression in one picture.
bulletPoints: Slope: roughly $110 per square foot on this data — a number a realtor can use
R² ≈ 0.50 with one feature: half the variance explained by size alone

agenda.title: Many Features, Many Units
agenda.description: Pipeline from Session 3, target = log(price), LinearRegression at the end. Coefficients now live on the log scale — a coefficient of 0.10 means roughly +10% price. Standardize to compare importance; never compare a per-square-foot slope to a per-garage-bay slope raw.
bulletPoints: log target: errors become percentage errors, so a 5% miss on a $100K house counts the same as on a $500K house
Predict, then np.expm1 to get back to dollars before you report RMSE

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, argue about what a garage is worth.

agenda.title: Overfitting & Regularization
agenda.description: Add polynomial terms and watch train R² climb while test R² collapses — the Overfitting Explorer, now with real houses. Then RidgeCV, LassoCV, ElasticNetCV: one alpha, chosen by cross-validation, and the coefficient path that shows lasso switching features off one by one.
bulletPoints: Ridge shrinks; lasso selects. Elastic net does both. Scale features first or the penalty is unfair
LassoCV keeps ~25 of 200+ one-hot columns on Ames: a model a client can read

agenda.title: Residual Diagnostics & the Metric Menu
agenda.description: Residuals vs. fitted: a fan means heteroscedasticity, a curve means a missing nonlinearity, a cluster of big misses means a segment the model doesn't understand. Then the metric menu — RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R² — and a one-line rule for which to report to whom.
bulletPoints: Report MAE to operations (typical miss), RMSE to risk (big misses matter), R² to statisticians, never MAPE near zero
Preview: HistGradientBoostingRegressor on the same pipeline drops RMSE by another 20% — Session 8

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Homework #2
agenda.description: The regression template: pipeline → log target → regularized linear model → residual plots → metrics in business units. HW2 is the Ames competition in miniature.
bulletPoints: HW2: a leak-proof Ames pipeline with ridge or lasso, due Mon Oct 19 (no class Oct 12)
Next: classification proper — logistic regression, kNN, and the confusion matrix in depth

activities.title: What Is a House Worth? Regularized Regression on Ames
activities.description: 1,460 house sales in Ames, Iowa, with 79 features. Build a leak-proof pipeline that predicts log(price), let LassoCV choose the penalty, and report the error in dollars a buyer would understand.

steps.title: Frame it
steps.description: Unit: one house. Target: sale price (modeled as log). Horizon: at listing. Decision: list price / offer price. Baseline: the mean price, RMSE ≈ $74K.

steps.title: Reuse the pipeline
steps.description: Session 3's ColumnTransformer, unchanged. Log-transform the target with np.log1p before fitting.

steps.title: Let CV pick alpha
steps.description: LassoCV(cv=5) at the end of the pipeline. Inspect how many coefficients survived and which features they are.

steps.title: Report in dollars
steps.description: Predict on the test set, np.expm1 the predictions, then RMSE and MAE in dollars. Plot residuals vs. fitted and describe the shape in one sentence.

codeBlock.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_openml
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, root_mean_squared_error

ames = fetch_openml('house_prices', as_frame=True)
X, y = ames.data.drop(columns=['Id']), ames.target
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=835)

# prep = the Session 3 ColumnTransformer (impute+scale numeric, one-hot categorical)
model = Pipeline([('prep', prep), ('lasso', LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=835))])
model.fit(X_tr, np.log1p(y_tr))

pred = np.expm1(model.predict(X_te))
print(f'Baseline RMSE (predict the mean): ${root_mean_squared_error(y_te, np.full(len(y_te), y_tr.mean())):,.0f}')
print(f'Lasso RMSE: ${root_mean_squared_error(y_te, pred):,.0f}   MAE: ${mean_absolute_error(y_te, pred):,.0f}')

coef = model.named_steps['lasso'].coef_
print(f'alpha chosen: {model.named_steps["lasso"].alpha_:.4f}, non-zero coefficients: {(coef != 0).sum()} of {len(coef)}')

activities.discussionNote: Look at which features lasso kept. Overall quality, living area, neighborhood dummies, year built — the list reads like a realtor's checklist, which is the point: a regularized linear model is the most explainable strong model you will ever ship. Then look at the residual plot: the biggest misses are the most expensive houses. The model knows less about a $450K house because it has seen fewer of them — and that is exactly the segment where a mistake costs the most.

takeaways.text: A linear coefficient is a slope in business units, holding other features fixed — not a cause, and not comparable across features until you standardize.
Ridge shrinks, lasso selects. Choose alpha by cross-validation, scale features first, and remember that a lasso model with 25 surviving features is one a client can read.

Metrics are for audiences: MAE for operations, RMSE when big misses hurt, R² for fit, MAPE never near zero. And always look at the residual plot — the fan shape is the log transform asking to be applied.
